a1-existence.title: There is/isn't: bor / yo'q
a1-existence.explanation: Bor and yo'q are standalone words that state whether something exists, with no verb "to be" involved at all: uyda non bor (there is bread at home), pulim yo'q (I don't have money, literally "my money doesn't-exist").
a1-existence.fact: Yo'q does double duty as both "there isn't/doesn't exist" and the everyday word for "no" in answer to a yes/no question -- the two uses come from exactly the same root idea of non-existence/negation.

dialogue.native: Yo'q, choy yo'q, faqat suv bor.
dialogue.en: No, there's no tea, only water.

a1-demonstratives.title: Demonstratives: bu / shu / u
a1-demonstratives.pattern: bu (this, near speaker) · shu (this, just mentioned) · u (that, far/absent)
a1-demonstratives.explanation: Bu points at something physically close to the speaker: bu kitob (this book, right here). U points at something distant or not present: u uy (that house, over there). Shu points back at something already mentioned in the conversation: shu masala (that matter [we were just discussing]).
a1-demonstratives.fact: Shu is the one English speakers most often reach for the wrong word for -- English "that" covers both u's distance and shu's "just-mentioned" sense, but Uzbek keeps them grammatically separate.

dialogue.en: Yes, I liked that book a lot.

items.en: There is a table in the room.
There are many trees in the garden.
There is no metro in this city.
Do you have an extra pen?
I don't have work right now.
